passages.happening:
The people call to one another. ‘Come, let us return to the LORD. For He has torn us to pieces, but He will heal us; He has wounded us, but He will bind up our wounds’ (verse 1). ‘After two days He will revive us; on the third day He will raise us up, that we may live in His presence’ (verse 2).

They urge each other to press on to know the LORD. They are sure he will come, ‘As surely as the sun rises’ (verse 3), like the rain, like the spring showers that water the earth.
passages.hearers:
Chapter 5 ended with God going back to his place until his people sought him. Now they answer, and the chapter is built as a dialogue: the people speak in verses 1 to 3, and God replies in verses 4 to 6. The people's words have the rhythm of a song or a prayer used in worship.

The pictures come from the farming year. Crops depended on the early rains of autumn and the late showers of spring, and the people compare God's coming to that dependable rain. Their confidence is real. They know the God who tears is the God who heals. What the song does not do is name any sin.

After two days, on the third day is a Hebrew way of saying after a short time. In its setting it speaks of the nation raised up again after God's judgment.
passages.later: The law had said that the LORD wounds and heals: ‘I bring death and I give life; I wound and I heal’ (Deuteronomy 32:39). Later prophets used the same picture of a people raised up, as in Ezekiel's valley of dry bones (Ezekiel 37:1-14).
passages.hard:
Is the people's song sincere, and does the third day point to Jesus?

Readers divide over these verses. Many read them as shallow repentance. The people assume God will heal them quickly and without fail, as surely as the sunrise, without confessing any particular sin, and God's reply in verse 4 shows how short-lived their loyalty is. Others read them as a true model prayer, the very seeking God was waiting for in 5:15, and hear God's reply as grief that even this will not last. The text supports something of both. The words are good, but Israel's history makes God doubt their staying power.

The third day raises a second question. Read in its setting, it speaks of Israel's revival after a short time, and some interpreters see no reference to Christ. Many Christian interpreters, from the early church onward, note that Paul says Christ was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:4) without naming a text, and think this verse is among those he had in mind. The New Testament never quotes it. These notes leave the connection as a reading, one of pattern rather than direct citation.
passages.asks: The people were sure God would heal them as surely as the sun rises. Ask whether you ever count on God's mercy without turning from anything. And ask what it would mean for you to press on to know the LORD, and not only to be helped by him.

passages.happening:
God answers with grief. ‘What shall I do with you, O Ephraim? What shall I do with you, O Judah? For your loyalty is like a morning mist, like the early dew that vanishes’ (verse 4). That is why he has cut them down by the prophets and his words of judgment have gone out like lightning (verse 5).

‘For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings’ (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
God's two questions sound like a parent at a loss. In the dry season of the land, heavy dew overnight and morning mist water the ground, but they burn off within hours. Israel's loyalty is like that: there at dawn and gone by noon. The people said God would come like the rain. God says their love is like the dew. The same picture of water measures the difference between his faithfulness and theirs.

The word rendered mercy is hesed, loving devotion, the loyal love of a covenant partner, the very thing God says is missing. Sacrifice was central to Israel's worship, commanded in the law. Hosea is not abolishing it. In Hebrew, a saying shaped as this, not that often means this more than that, as the second line shows: the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings. The prophets say again and again that sacrifice without faithfulness is worthless.
passages.later: Samuel told Saul, ‘obedience is better than sacrifice’ (1 Samuel 15:22), and Micah asks what the LORD requires (Micah 6:6-8). Jesus quoted verse 6 twice. When he ate with tax collectors and sinners he said, ‘But go and learn what this means’ (Matthew 9:13), and when his disciples were condemned for picking grain on the Sabbath he said they would not have condemned the innocent if they had known it (Matthew 12:7).
passages.asks: God wants loyal love more than offerings. Ask whether your religion has become a list of things done for God in place of knowing him. And Jesus used this verse against people who kept the rules and despised sinners. Ask where that warning falls on you.

passages.t: Covenant broken: Adam, Gilead and Shechem
passages.happening:
‘But they, like Adam, have transgressed the covenant; there they were unfaithful to Me’ (verse 7). ‘Gilead is a city of evildoers, tracked with footprints of blood’ (verse 8). A band of priests lies in ambush like raiders and murders on the road to Shechem (verse 9). In the house of Israel God has seen a horrible thing: Ephraim's prostitution, and Israel defiled (verse 10).

Judah too has a harvest appointed, when God restores his people's fortunes (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The chapter belongs to the troubled 730s BC, when Israel suffered Assyrian invasion and violence within. The places in verses 7 to 10 point to events now mostly lost. Gilead, east of the Jordan, was home to the fifty men who helped Pekah murder King Pekahiah in Samaria, which may be why Hosea calls it a city tracked with blood. Shechem was an ancient city in the hill country and a city of refuge, and the road to it was apparently the scene of murders involving priests.

The word Adam in verse 7 is read two ways. It may be the town of Adam on the Jordan, where the river's waters stood in a heap when Israel crossed into the land; the word there that follows suggests a place, and some scholars think Hosea means a covenant-breaking event at that town, though nothing more is known of it. The BSB's like Adam reads it as the first man, who also broke God's command. Both readings are defended.

Verse 11 turns to Judah. Its harvest may be judgment, or it may belong with the restoration in the same line. Translations differ, and some join it to the start of chapter 7.
passages.later: At the town of Adam the waters of the Jordan stood in a heap (Joshua 3:16). Shechem was one of the cities of refuge (Joshua 20:7), and Gilead was home to the men who helped Pekah kill Pekahiah (2 Kings 15:25).
passages.asks: Even the priests had become killers. Ask what happens to a community when those who should protect people prey on them. And ask whether you are keeping the covenant in the ordinary places of your life, where no one is watching.
